changes.before: Change input text to "12x". What happens with this strict validation?
changes.after: strtol turns the start of text into a long integer. Check where it stopped before accepting the number.

before: const char *text points to text that this code will not modify through that pointer. strtol converts the initial number into long and stores a pointer to the first unconverted character through an end-pointer argument. char *end declares such a pointer; &end passes its address so strtol can update it.
end==text means no digits were converted. *end reads the character at that position; requiring it to be '\0' rejects trailing nonnumeric text in this strict policy.
Set errno=0 before calling strtol. ERANGE reports an out-of-range conversion. errno belongs to errno.h; do not infer failure from a legitimate numeric zero result alone.
Base 10 requests decimal. A cast to int would still need a separate int-range check; this program keeps the long result.
Expected output or behavior: 12. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

Optional local transfer task: Trace "0", "x", and "12x" separately. Distinguish a legitimate zero from missing digits. You may trace it without a C compiler; reading completion is not proof of a local run.
after: `strtol` reads a number from text. It returns a long value. `const char *text` is a pointer to characters this code will not change through that pointer. `char *end` will point to where number reading stopped.

`&end` gives strtol the address of end so it can update that pointer. If `end == text`, no digits were read. `*end` reads the character where it stopped. This program accepts the text only if that character is the ending zero.

`errno` stores certain library error reports. Set it to 0 before calling strtol. `ERANGE` means the number is outside long's range. A returned value of zero alone does not mean failure; zero is a valid number too.
The input 10 selects decimal numbers, the usual base-ten system. Keep the answer as long here. To store it in int, you would first need to check that it fits int's smaller or equal range.
The text contains only the number 12. Digits were read, the ending was reached, and the value fits. The program prints 12.
Change the text to 12x. strtol reads 12 but stops at x. This program rejects any leftover character, including a space after the number.
